node.label: Sara Ahmed
node.date_label: Strange Encounters (2000) · The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004) · Queer Phenomenology (2006) · The Promise of Happiness (2010) · Living a Feminist Life (2017)
node.description: A feminist theorist of emotion, orientation and institutional life. The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004) asks what emotions do: Ahmed traces how they are named in speech acts and felt on the skin, and how they work in debates on terrorism, asylum, migration and reconciliation. In “Affective Economies” (2004), she argues that emotions circulate between bodies and signs, helping form the boundaries of individual and collective bodies. Queer Phenomenology (2006) reads Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty and Fanon with queer and critical race theory to show how bodies are oriented toward some objects and away from others. The Promise of Happiness (2010) treats happiness as a promise that directs lives toward some choices and away from others; its figures include the feminist killjoy, the unhappy queer, the angry Black woman and the melancholic migrant. A 2010 Signs article proposes that feminist histories might offer an alternative history of happiness. Ahmed reused Judith Butler’s definition of performativity to describe the non-performativity of words such as “diversity”, which do not bring about what they name. She names Stuart Hall and Angela Davis as formative for how she takes race seriously, and she criticises Julia Kristeva’s account of French universalism and the Muslim headscarf. Reviewing Strange Encounters (2000), Julie Wuthnow called it an original contribution to postcolonial, cultural and feminist theory, but found that its chapter on global feminism underplays the power and antagonism stressed earlier in the book.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Strange Encounters: Embodied Others in Post-Coloniality (2000); The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004; second edition 2014); Queer Phenomenology: Orientations, Objects, Others (2006); The Promise of Happiness (2010); “Killing Joy: Feminism and the History of Happiness” (2010); On Being Included: Racism and Diversity in Institutional Life (2012); Living a Feminist Life (2017).
node.scope_note: Ahmed’s own essays on her website (2014–2023) and “Feminist Killjoys” (2010) were read in full; the 2004 discussion of Kristeva is read only as she reproduces it in a 2015 essay. “Affective Economies” (2004) was read on the author’s own site in selected pages 117–121. The books are unread: they are described from publisher pages (Duke, Edinburgh) and, for Strange Encounters, from one open review. The Signs article is represented by its repository abstract only. Repository copies of “Orientations Matter” and “Problematic Proximities” are access-restricted and were not read.

chronology.interpretation: Argument claims rest on Ahmed’s own essays, publisher descriptions, one review and one abstract, each with the reading limits recorded on the edges.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Effort to Transform” (2017), written on Hall’s intellectual legacies, Ahmed says that reading Hall’s “Cultural Identity and Diaspora” during her PhD “changed everything”, taught her to think about identity from her own experience, and showed her how cultural studies could be turned on the university; though she spoke to him only once, she calls Hall her teacher through his texts.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ahmed’s own 2017 essay, paragraphs on her PhD reading and the two closing paragraphs before the notes. She distinguishes Hall’s teaching through his words from having been taught by him personally and records only one conversation. This is stated intellectual debt, not supervision.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hall’s diaspora essay as a lifelong companion text

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Effort to Transform” (2017) Ahmed names Angela Davis among the Black feminist writers whose texts “changed everything” for her during her PhD, and says that Davis and Stuart Hall made her aware of what it means to take race seriously as an object of thought.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Same complete post. Opening paragraph: Ahmed introduced Davis at a 2014 conference on Hall’s legacies. Paragraph beginning “But then in the second year of my PhD I read a series of texts by black feminists and feminists of colour (including Angela Davis, Audre Lorde and Gloria Anzaldúa)”; paragraph beginning “Both Angela Davis and Stuart Hall made me aware of what it means to take race seriously as an object of thought.” Corroboration of engagement with Davis’s argument: “A Feminist Army” (2016), paragraph beginning “A call of arms is thus a recall”, uses Women, Race and Class on Sojourner Truth’s speech. Davis is named with Lorde and Anzaldúa; no claim that she is Ahmed’s only source. Davis’s books not reread here.
proposed_edges.map_label: Black feminist texts that changed everything

proposed_edges.relationship: Introducing a 2023 public conversation with Butler, Ahmed says she reused Butler’s definition of performativity from Bodies That Matter (1993) to describe what she called non-performativity, words such as “diversity” that do not bring into effect what they name, and that Butler’s work “keeps teaching” her.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ahmed’s written introduction, posted on her own site on 26 July 2023, to a conversation with Butler at Cambridge on 28 April 2023. Paragraph beginning “A conversation needs a space. A conversation is a space”: “I think of how I reused your definition of performativity from Bodies that Matter to describe what I called non-performativity: how words do not bring into effect what they name (words like diversity, for instance).” Paragraph beginning “To be in conversation with someone else’s work”: “You keep teaching me in your work”. Paragraph beginning “And yes we do laugh”: “Judith taught me that we need to be in trouble”. A stated conceptual debt. Ahmed’s non-performativity essays and Bodies That Matter not reread here; the recorded conversation was not heard.

proposed_edges.relationship: Queer Phenomenology (2006) reads Fanon with Husserl, Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty in building a queer model of orientation; in a 2014 essay revisiting that book Ahmed writes that from Fanon “we learn about the experience of disorientation” under the white gaze.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Duke University Press description of Queer Phenomenology: “she combines readings of phenomenological texts—by Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, and Fanon—with insights drawn from queer studies, feminist theory, critical race theory, Marxism, and psychoanalysis.” Ahmed, “Queer Angles” (2014), paragraph beginning “From Frantz Fanon, we learn about the experience of disorientation, as the experience of being an object amongst other objects”, citing Black Skin, White Masks; the preceding paragraph refers to the conclusion of Queer Phenomenology. Corroboration: “Being in Question” (2014), paragraphs beginning “When we are in question we question” (“This was after all how Frantz Fanon proceeded”) and “For Fanon, ontology is impossible.” The book itself and “A Phenomenology of Whiteness” (2007) are unread; the 2006 claim rests on the publisher description, the debt on Ahmed’s own 2014 essays.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the chapter on love in The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004), reproduced in her 2015 essay “Melancholic Universalism”, Ahmed criticises Kristeva’s Nations without Nationalism (1993), arguing that Kristeva’s abstract French national ideal in fact takes the shape of particular bodies and requires the veiled Muslim woman to give up her difference.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ahmed’s own 2015 post reproduces her 2004 passage. Paragraph beginning “I first offered reflections on this theme in my book, The Cultural Politics of Emotion published over 10 years ago in 2004. It was in the chapter on love. I referred specifically to the work of Julia Kristeva.” Quoted passage: “However, the argument that the national idea is abstract (and the difference of the Muslim woman is concrete) breaks down”; “In Kristeva’s text, moving towards the abstract promise of the nation requires moving away from the veiled woman”. She also partly follows Kristeva (“I would follow Kristeva by arguing that the nation is hence an effect of how bodies move towards it”), so this is a qualified critique. Kristeva’s book not reread; the 2004 book read only in Ahmed’s reproduction.
proposed_edges.map_label: Kristeva’s national ideal is not abstract

proposed_edges.relationship: According to Julie Wuthnow’s 2002 review, Strange Encounters (2000) deploys Marx’s notion of commodity fetishism to link the representation of strangers to broader relationships of production, framing its argument as a critique of “stranger fetishism”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sociological Research Online review, complete. Paragraph beginning “The notion that the Self constructs itself”: Ahmed augments the self–other approach first “through her deployment of Marx’s notion of commodity fetishism, which motivates her to attempt to ‘demonstrate the links between representation and broader relationships of production’ (61).” Opening paragraph quotes Ahmed (p. 6) on avoiding “stranger fetishism”. A reviewer’s account of the book’s method, with a page reference; the book is unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Feminist Killjoys” (2010) Ahmed places her figure of the feminist killjoy in the context of feminist critiques of happiness and quotes Beauvoir’s The Second Sex (1949) on how easy it is to call happy a situation in which one wishes to place others; a 2014 essay reports Beauvoir’s reading of Mrs Dalloway’s parties.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: S&F Online 8.3 (2010), section “Killjoys”, paragraph beginning “The figure of the feminist killjoy makes sense if we place her in the context of feminist critiques of happiness”: “As Simone de Beauvoir described so astutely ‘it is always easy to describe as happy a situation in which one wishes to place [others]’” (n. 4, The Second Sex, p. 28). “Dated Feminists” (2014), paragraph beginning “Much of the book is about an event that will happen”: “For Simone de Beauvoir, Mrs. Dalloway’s enjoyment of parties is read as a sign that she is trying to turn her ‘prison into glory’” (p. 554). Supplementary: Wuthnow’s 2002 review places Strange Encounters in a self–other line of social theory running from The Second Sex and Orientalism, which Ahmed “augments”. THIN: two body-text uses of Beauvoir as a resource for one argument, not a stated debt; flag for the outside reviewers. The Promise of Happiness itself unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Queer Phenomenology (2006) proposes a queer model of orientations, examining how bodies are directed toward some objects and away from others and how queerness reorders those spatial relations; Ahmed’s 2014 essay “Queer Angles” extends its account of bodies “out of line”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Duke description (a single paragraph beginning “In this groundbreaking work, Sara Ahmed demonstrates how queer studies can put phenomenology to productive use”): “A queer phenomenology, Ahmed contends, reveals how social relations are arranged spatially, how queerness disrupts and reorders these relations by not following the accepted paths”; “Queer Phenomenology points queer theory in bold new directions.” “Queer Angles” (2014), paragraph beginning “By implication, then”: “I observed in the conclusion to Queer Phenomenology, how we can become what disorientates the picture, a body out of line.” Publisher description plus the author’s own restatement; book unread. Contribution to queer theory, not a claim about historians’ use of it.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Killing Joy: Feminism and the History of Happiness” (Signs, 2010) Ahmed suspends the belief that happiness is good, a belief she treats as central to the intellectual history of happiness, and proposes that feminist histories might offer an alternative history of happiness; The Promise of Happiness (2010) works through that intellectual history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Goldsmiths repository abstract of the Signs article: “It proceeds by suspending belief that happiness is a good thing, or that happiness is what we want, as beliefs that are central to the intellectual history of happiness. The article suggests that feminist histories might offer an alternative history of happiness.” Duke description of The Promise of Happiness: “Ahmed draws on the intellectual history of happiness, from classical accounts of ethics as the good life” through nineteenth-century utilitarianism. Abstract and publisher description only; article body unread (DOI page 403, JSTOR JavaScript wall). The atlas node already notes that Ahmed’s affect inquiry needs separate research; this edge claims only her proposal of a feminist history of happiness, not adoption by historians of emotion.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ahmed describes taking the tools of cultural studies, learned from Stuart Hall, into ethnographic research on diversity work in universities, treating the university as a place to work on as well as at; the publisher describes The Promise of Happiness (2010) as combining philosophy and feminist cultural studies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: “The Effort to Transform” (2017), paragraph beginning “I take seriously Stuart Hall’s suggestion”: “I began to think of how cultural studies provides the tools to interrogate the university as a place to work on as well as work at”; paragraph beginning “Why practical phenomenology?”: “This is what I learnt from doing ethnographic research on diversity within universities.” Duke description of The Promise of Happiness: “Combining philosophy and feminist cultural studies”. Self-description plus publisher description; On Being Included (2012) not read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Cultural studies turned on the university

proposed_edges.relationship: Strange Encounters: Embodied Others in Post-Coloniality (2000) argues that the stranger is not simply whoever is unfamiliar but a figure produced by processes of inclusion and exclusion; Julie Wuthnow’s 2002 review called it an original contribution to postcolonial, cultural and feminist theory, while judging that its closing chapter on global feminism underplays the power and antagonism stressed earlier.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sociological Research Online review, complete. Opening paragraph: “makes an original and insightful contribution to postcolonial, cultural and feminist theory”; Ahmed quoted (p. 6): “we need to consider how the stranger is an effect of processes of inclusion and exclusion”. Fourth paragraph, beginning “Finally, I found that her most ‘visionary’ chapter”: the reviewer’s criticism of the global-feminism chapter. A reviewer’s assessment; book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Witness to History: Conversation with Leading Scholars (2020; transcript posted in 2021), Adele Perry draws on Sara Ahmed’s politics of citation to propose changing whose perspectives historians read and elevate in their research and teaching.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Perry’s answer and surrounding discussion in the organizer-publisher’s transcript. Perry explicitly attributes the idea to Ahmed and explains its use in choosing whose scholarship receives attention. This supports a specific methodological uptake, not a claim about Perry’s whole historical project. Perry names no particular Ahmed publication, so none is supplied. The accompanying event page dates the discussion to 26 November 2020 and its online posting to 9 February 2021.
proposed_edges.map_label: Politics of citation applied to historians’ practice

proposed_edges.relationship: In 'More-Than-Human Emotional Communities' (2020), Thomas Webb, Chris Pearson, Penny Summerfield and Mark Riley invoke Sara Ahmed's insight from 'Affective Economies' (2004) that 'emotions do things' to explain how soldier–mule bonds helped sustain British forces in Burma.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the abstract and introductory methodological discussion, numbered pp. 1–5, in Summerfield’s institutional repository. The body explicitly uses Ahmed’s insight to explain the practical effects of soldier–mule bonds, and note 14 identifies the source. The claim belongs to the four authors collectively; it is not evidence of Summerfield’s individual contribution to the coauthored argument. The manuscript distinguishes this use from its central borrowing of Rosenwein’s emotional-community concept. The complete article and Ahmed’s cited article were not read for this edge.
proposed_edges.map_label: Affective economies applied to soldier–mule bonds
